title: Staff outside civil-service hiring, and outside the unions
question: What share of each department’s staff holds an exempt appointment rather than a permanent civil-service one, how has that moved, and how many are in classes no union represents?
finding: The payroll file does record a type of appointment for every row from fiscal 2017. On that record, exempt appointments were 14.0% of City staff time in fiscal 2017 and 13.2% in fiscal 2026: 2,570 full-time equivalents on permanent exempt appointments (2,379 in fiscal 2017) and 2,165 on temporary exempt ones (2,304 in fiscal 2017). Provisional appointments went from 48 to 194 full-time equivalents. 102 people were paid in classes the file marks as unrepresented. The exempt share rose most in Human Rights Commission (14.9% to 66.8%) and Emergency Management (4.8% to 20.3%).
how: City payroll file, fiscal 2017 to 2026. The file’s “employment type” column takes the values Permanent Civil Service, Permanent Exempt, Temporary Exempt, Temporary Provisional and Other. Staff time is hours paid divided by the paid hours of a full-time year in that fiscal year, read off the file (2,080 in most years, 2,160 in fiscal 2026), so that seasonal and occasional workers count for what they work. Unrepresented means the union column reads “Unrepresented” (management or miscellaneous). Departments under 20 full-time equivalents are left out, as are board seats, elected offices and the Superior Court, whose staff the file shows as exempt throughout. Ranked by the rise in the exempt share. The classes column gives the largest permanent exempt classes, with full-time equivalents.
limits: On exempt appointment: the City Charter (section 10.104) sets out 19 categories of worker excluded from competitive selection, as the civil grand jury’s 2023 report describes. The payroll shows whole offices, such as the City Attorney’s and the Mayor’s, as almost entirely exempt, which is consistent with posts exempt by category rather than one by one. The payroll gives the broad type only. It does not say which Charter category a post falls under, whether a category has a cap, or whether the post was advertised; the exempt-appointment reports would. The civil grand jury’s 2023 finding that the City over-uses temporary exempt positions is quoted in the waivers and exceptions screens and is not repeated here.
